crop_profile.summary: Wheat (Triticum aestivum) is a globally important annual cereal grown on loamy to clay soils with pH 6.0-7.5. Optimal temperatures are 10-25 °C, rainfall 300-900 mm/year, and sunlight 6-10 h/day. It requires medium water and nitrogen, with critical moisture needs during flowering. Major producers include China, India, Russia, the United States, and France. Typical yields are 3 t/ha, reaching up to 7 t/ha under optimal management. Key diseases are Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and leaf rust; main pests include aphids, Hessian fly, and wheat midge. Integrated pest management, split nitrogen fertilization, and timely harvest ensure high quality grain.

actions: 1. Field inspection: Walk the field today; look for Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and other nutrient deficiency symptoms; record affected areas.
2. Immediate irrigation: Apply surface or sprinkler irrigation today to raise soil moisture to field capacity; repeat every 2‑3 days until NDWI improves (target >0.3).
3. Mulching/shading: Lay a 5‑10 cm layer of straw or biodegradable mulch over the row furrows to lower soil temperature and reduce evaporation.
4. Organic amendment: Incorporate well‑composted organic manure (≈5 t/ha) within the next 7 days to raise organic carbon and improve moisture retention.
5. Nitrogen management: Conduct a quick leaf‑chlorophyll test; if nitrogen is still limiting, apply a split dose of urea (≈50 kg N/ha) within 3 days, monitoring for leaching risk.
6. Record keeping: Log irrigation volumes, mulch coverage, and any disease observations in a field notebook or mobile app.

steps.finding: Conduct an immediate field inspection and implement urgent water‑stress mitigation and soil‑health measures (irrigation, mulching, organic amendment, and calibrated nitrogen application).
actions: 1. Field inspection: Walk the field today; look for Fusarium head blight, powdery mildew, and other nutrient deficiency symptoms; record affected areas.
2. Immediate irrigation: Apply surface or sprinkler irrigation today to raise soil moisture to field capacity; repeat every 2‑3 days until NDWI improves (target >0.3).
3. Mulching/shading: Lay a 5‑10 cm layer of straw or biodegradable mulch over the row furrows to lower soil temperature and reduce evaporation.
4. Organic amendment: Incorporate well‑composted organic manure (≈5 t/ha) within the next 7 days to raise organic carbon and improve moisture retention.
5. Nitrogen management: Conduct a quick leaf‑chlorophyll test; if nitrogen is still limiting, apply a split dose of urea (≈50 kg N/ha) within 3 days, monitoring for leaching risk.
6. Record keeping: Log irrigation volumes, mulch coverage, and any disease observations in a field notebook or mobile app.
steps.justification: Temperatures (30 °C) far exceed wheat's optimal range and rainfall is far below the required 300‑900 mm/year, causing severe moisture deficit (NDWI near zero) and critical vegetation health (NDVI 0.15). Soil is otherwise excellent (optimal pH, high nitrogen, clay‑loam texture) but low organic carbon reduces water‑holding capacity. Prompt inspection, supplemental irrigation, and soil amendments are needed to prevent irreversible yield loss.
